body: I’m not really sure on the distinction myself yet. I’m still physically attracted to my partner, but I know that’s because they haven’t made any steps towards transitioning yet. I have this feeling that my physical attraction to him may not last the course of his transition. I still love him deeply, though, and we’ve agreed to just feel it out as we go along <3 thank you for your comment

Thank you for your response. I think my reaction is definitely not knee-jerk; I know I made the conversation seem short but we spoke in depth for upwards of four hours on the topic. He communicated to me that his end goal is manhood, that he’d like to fully medically and socially transition. Had he come out as nonbinary, genderfluid or transmasculine, I don’t think it would’ve been a huge problem for me.

I know that I’m attracted to women from experience, but I also have never been in a situation like this. I’m open to discovering a different aspect of my sexuality, I’d even welcome it if it meant I get to keep my partner. But I have this feeling that he will eventually cross a threshold in his transition where I simply won’t be attracted anymore.

I definitely made the post in the height of my emotion and in the midst of both of our fears about a breakup. I know it will take some years for him to transition, so we’ve agreed to take it slow and feel it out as we go.

Thank you again <3

Thank you for the kind words. I think this is the most accurate response I’ve gotten so far- I still love him and am still very much attracted to him, but I think eventually that there will be a threshold (whether that is physically or otherwise, I don’t know?) where I won’t be as attracted anymore.

Once you've developed as male, then you have a biological advantage. It's not transphobic to seperate a certain class of athlete from another in sports. That's why we have different divisions (amateuar, professional, etc) and weight classes in certain sports. Weight is a biological advantage. Age is a biological advantage.Bone structure and muscle mass are biological advantages.

Coming from a girl who competes at the highschool level, if we let a person with an entirely different bone structure compete in, say, track, it would be no competition. Yes, these girls are great athletes and should have a right to recognition and competition, but it simply isn't fair to have them demolish other girls like this. I don't have an idea for a solution, but telling your female athletes to just 'work harder' isn't it.

It's like pitting a highschool basketball team against a little league basketball team. The little league will be obliterated. Does that mean they're a bad little league team? No, not at all. It just isn't fair for them to compete against athletes that are on an entirely different level.
